theme: The garden, the man, the woman; the covenant of works arranged
settingTheScene:
Genesis 2 is not a second, contradictory creation story. It is a deliberate narrowing, a re-telling that zooms in on Day 6 of Chapter 1 to show us how humanity, in particular, was made and where humanity was placed. In Hebrew literary form, this kind of telescoping is common: first a wide overview, then a closer look at the part that matters most for the story to follow.

What follows in the Bible, the Fall, the covenants, the long history of redemption, only makes sense if we understand what humanity was originally meant to be and where humanity was originally meant to live. Genesis 2 sets up the covenant relationship between God and Adam that the next chapter will catastrophically break.
observation: The name “LORD God” (Yahweh Elohim) appears here for the first time. Genesis 1 used Elohim, the general word for God. Now we encounter God’s covenant name combined with that title, the same God, but now revealed in personal relationship.
God forms man from the dust and breathes into his nostrils. Humanity is both earthly (made of the same material as the ground) and uniquely alive with God’s own breath.
The garden is described in beautiful detail, trees pleasant to the sight and good for food, a river that divides into four headwaters. This is paradise, but it is also a real place.
There are two named trees: the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The command not to eat from the second is the first command God gives to humanity.
Adam is told to “work and keep” the garden. These same two Hebrew verbs are later used of the priests’ service in the Tabernacle. Adam is, in a sense, the first priest.

The making of the woman is preceded by Adam discovering that nothing in creation corresponds to him. The woman is made from his side, not from his head to rule him or his feet to be ruled, but from his side as his equal partner.
interpretation:
Genesis 2 reveals that the creation account is, at its heart, a covenant account. The setting is a garden, Eden, but the garden is more than a beautiful place. It is the temple of creation, the meeting place between God and humanity, the original holy ground. The river that flows out of it waters the world, suggesting that what happens in this garden is meant to spread outward, that the holiness and life of God’s presence is meant to extend to the ends of the earth.

Into this garden God places the man, and the words used to describe his task are loaded. He is to “work” and “keep” it, the same words later used of the priests who served in the Tabernacle. Adam is given a role that is simultaneously royal (exercising dominion) and priestly (serving and guarding the sacred space). He is a king-priest in a garden-temple, representing God to creation and creation to God.

Then comes the command. “Of every tree of the garden you may surely eat, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die.” Notice the structure: God’s generosity comes first (“of every tree… you may surely eat”) and the one prohibition follows. This is the pattern of all true covenant relationship with God. Grace and gift come first; obedience is the response. The single commandment is not God being stingy or cruel. It is the test of whether Adam will trust God’s wisdom about good and evil, or whether he will reach out and try to define those things for himself.

This arrangement is what theologians have long called the covenant of works. God offered Adam a relationship of life and blessing on the condition of obedience. Had Adam obeyed, he would have come into the fullness of what God offered, life confirmed, blessing extended, perhaps eventually access to the tree of life itself. But the conditional nature of the arrangement also meant that disobedience would bring death. The stakes were not arbitrary; they were the natural consequence of either trusting God or refusing to.

Then the narrative slows down again. God observes that “it is not good that the man should be alone.” This is the first thing in creation declared not good, and it is not a flaw in creation, but a deliberate setup. Adam needs to discover his own lack before he receives the gift of a partner. So God brings the animals, and Adam names them, exercising his dominion, but also noticing that none of them correspond to him. None is a true partner.

So God puts Adam into a deep sleep, takes a rib from his side, and forms the woman. Adam’s response is the first poetry in the Bible: “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” Marriage is established before the Fall, before sin enters the world. It is part of God’s original good design, a covenant between a man and a woman that pictures, in its own way, the deeper covenant between God and his people. The chapter ends with the haunting line: “And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.” There was no fear, no hiding, no covering. That is the world we lost.
connection: Yesterday we saw God speak the cosmos into existence. Today we see him stoop to the dust and form a man with his own hands. The same God who is transcendent over creation is also intimate with his creatures. This is the God whose Son will later “take on flesh and dwell among us,” who will gather children in his arms, who will form a new humanity from his pierced side as Adam’s bride was formed from his. The pattern of Genesis 2, a man, a garden, a tree, a bride, will echo throughout Scripture all the way to the new creation in Revelation 22, where the tree of life appears again, and the river flows again, and the bride of Christ is finally united to her husband forever.
application:
If you are tempted today to think God is distant or impersonal, return to Genesis 2. The God of the Bible is not aloof. He kneels in the dust to form humanity. He plants a garden by hand. He breathes his own life into Adam’s nostrils. He notices when his creature is alone and provides for him. This is the kind of God you serve.

Practically, consider three things today. First, your body is not a problem, it is part of God’s design, formed by God himself. Treat it as such. Second, work is not a curse from the Fall; it was given before sin entered. The work you do this week is part of God’s image-bearing commission. Do it well. Third, the relationships God has given you, spouse, family, friends, church, are reflections of the original “it is not good for man to be alone.” You were not made for isolation. Show up. Be present. Let the people God has put in your life see your face without shame, as far as it is possible.
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 2:4-25 slowly. Genesis 1 gave a wide view of creation; this chapter zooms in on the garden, the man, and the woman. Notice what God provides, what he commands, and the one thing he calls “not good.” Read it aloud if you can.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for making you a creature with a body, a place, and relationships, and tell him if any of that is hard to receive as a gift.
Ask him to show you what he has placed in your care.
Speak to him about any place where you are tempted to doubt his good word.
